Winning high-value projects with better estimate follow-up

Panel upgrades, EV chargers and commercial fit-outs are decided after the estimate is sent. A breakdown of the follow-up system that wins more of them.

Big jobs are decided slowly

A service call is booked on the phone. A panel upgrade, an EV charger installation or a commercial fit-out is decided over days or weeks, often by more than one person. The estimate is the start of the sale, not the end of it.

Yet many electrical contractors treat a sent estimate as a finished task. If the customer doesn’t reply, the opportunity quietly expires.

The cost of that silence is easy to underestimate. A single signed panel upgrade or commercial fit-out can be worth as much as dozens of service calls, and the marketing spend to win the enquiry has already been paid. Improving follow-up is often the cheapest way for an electrical contractor to grow revenue from the same lead volume.

The system

1. Send the estimate with a next step

Every estimate should end with a clear next step and a date: “I’ll call you Thursday to go through the options.” That turns a one-way document into a conversation.

2. Make every touch useful

Follow-up works when it helps the customer decide. Answer the question they didn’t ask, explain what’s included, share a relevant project photo, or offer a phased option.

  • A short video walking through the estimate.
  • A comparison of good, better and best options.
  • Information on permits, timelines and what to expect on install day.
  • Financing or phasing for larger projects.

3. Give every estimate an owner

An estimate with no owner is an estimate nobody follows up. Assign one person, add tasks to the CRM, and review open estimates weekly.

“Most lost estimates aren’t lost to a competitor. They’re lost to silence.”

Commercial projects need a longer runway

Facility managers and general contractors work to budgets and approval cycles. Ask about their timeline early and match follow-up to it. A check-in when their budget opens is worth more than three emails in the first week.

In practice · Electrical

A shared “open estimates” board reviewed every Monday, sorted by value, with the next touch and owner for each line.

Measure what matters

Estimate metrics worth tracking
MetricWhy it matters
Estimate-to-signed rateThe clearest sign of sales effectiveness
Days from estimate to decisionShows how long follow-up needs to last
Open estimates with no next stepThe leak you can fix this week
Signed value by lead sourceTells marketing where big jobs come from

Let marketing see what happens after the estimate

Marketing usually stops at the lead. But for high-value work, the lead is only the first step, and the channels that produce the most estimates are not always the ones that produce signed projects. When estimate outcomes are tagged with their original source, marketing can focus spend on the channels that bring buyers, not just enquiries.

The same data improves the message. If commercial clients consistently ask about scheduling around business hours, put that answer on the landing page. If homeowners hesitate at the price of a panel upgrade, explain financing before the estimate, not after it.

Over time, follow-up becomes a source of insight as well as revenue: every lost estimate with a recorded reason is a small piece of research into why customers choose someone else.

Start here

  1. List every open estimate over a set value and assign an owner.
  2. Write a three-touch follow-up for your most common project type.
  3. Track signed rate by source for the next 90 days.

Key takeaways

  • High-value projects take longer to decide, so follow-up must last longer.
  • Each touch should add something: an answer, an option, a reassurance.
  • One owner per open estimate prevents silent drop-off.
  • Track estimate-to-signed rate by source and by job type.
